utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're sitting today until 1.00 or perhaps a few minutes after. What we'll do is this: We'll hear the evidence for about an hour and a quarter, then at 10.15 we'll take a break for quarter of an hour, another hour and a quarter or so and a second quarter of an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the document of the witness, we're at page 32, paragraph 219, and tab 42 in the bundle. If the bundle could be before the witness. I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, I think, is a transcript of a conversation between you and General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the wording of what was said when we both came out of the courtyard, having seen what was in there, and there was then a requirement to -- to brief the press, which General Loncar and I did together, and this was a note that was made by one of the officers with me, which was then written up straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You express the view in your statement that, as we can see on the second page of this if it's placed on the overhead projector, General Loncar expressing Racak concerns or Racak-like concerns, you taking the view that you weren't going to mention Racak.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was very conscious that there were -- while there were some similarities, there were also some very substantial differences and that it wasn't going to assist anybody to -- to start comparing this event with Racak, which had already achieved a notoriety of its own. And so the one thing I was trying not to do was to escalate the situation further. However, I was extremely keen that there should be a proper investigation of this event because, while there were differences, it was certainly not an open and closed case, as far as I could see. Only four of the deceased had actually been in any semblance of insurgent uniform - that is, four of the 25 - only 12 weapons were there; and the exchange rate for people who appeared -- who were alleged to have fought back, that of 25 dead and no wounded on the one side for one dead on the other struck me as remarkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the first sheet, we see your recording General Loncar as asserting in the briefing, as it were, that all of them were armed, and these civilian terrorists, according to their clothes, we cannot say they did not use weapons.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I think was touched on yesterday, this incident, grave as it may have been, was somewhat lost in the events that followed. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had hoped that the Finnish forensic team which had been prevailed upon to carry out the investigation of the -- of the bodies from Racak could be persuaded to stay on and to carry out investigations here. This proved not to be the case, and they were withdrawn within days of -- in fact, within a day of this event. So that was not possible. Moreover, the next day, we started to get members of the Contact Group arriving to discuss the aftermath of Racak. And while I briefed this incident to various people that came in, as you say, it was swallowed up and was never fully followed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next few paragraphs, indeed to the end of the document that you're referring to, I'm going to be selective as to passages. If you'd be good enough to follow me.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On paragraph 221 and on the 16th of March at a meeting in the Pristina barracks --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- you were expecting new MUP liaisons - the last line, really - as part of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken into the barracks and introduced to a number of new liaison officers, a very large number of new liaison officers, and this seemed to be a change to all the practices that had evolved over the previous month. We were certainly expecting to have about an equal number of police and army liaison officers. In the event, they were all army liaison officers, which surprised me somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And suggested a shift --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of emphasis.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got the impression from this that the army were taking the lead in -- in the -- in the campaign from that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At paragraph 222, at about the same time, within a day or so, you were introduced to serving General Brankovic, supposed to be retired General Loncar's replacement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I got the very firm impression that a different personality with a different relationship to us had been introduced and that Loncar was going to be replaced by someone who was who was going to, I got the impression, be even more hard-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 224. Evacuation started or occurred on the 20th of March, although it was sadly incomplete as to the evacuation of computer hard drives containing personnel lists.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every office had a computer. All of the areas that I was responsible for removed hard drives and ensured that nothing was left behind which could -- could identify individuals who had been our civilian employees. Sadly, our administrative section, I understand, neglected to do that, and a list of our civilian employees was left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Sandra Mitchell, who is the person who may be able to help the Chamber most with the preparation of the OSCE published reports, is also the person who will be able to deal with the possible consequences of that oversight.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 226. Going back in time and covering matters not absolutely sequentially from now on, in February, had your conversations with Colonel Kotur led to certain possible implications or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a mix of my conversations with Colonel Kotur and also Richard Ciaglinski's conversations. But between himself and myself - and I believe he will be coming to this court - we gained the very firm impression that there was planning going on for a VJ major offensive against the KLA throughout Kosovo and that this was planned to take place as and when the Kosovo Verification Mission departed. I have to explain that one of the things we were clear about was that if the violence got to a certain level, then we would have to withdraw the Kosovo Verification Mission, not least because the participating states of the OSCE were particularly concerned for the safety of -- of their people. And therefore, there was a level of violence above which the OSCE was not prepared to operate with an unarmed mission; and clearly, when we were starting to get people wounded, this became a matter of some concern, and so the evacuation plan was something which was always available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 227 contains expressions of views on topics that are, of course, ultimately for this Chamber and may be the subject of other opinions by others, but I'll ask you to deal with it, not least because it may be thought to be something the accused would want. But you surveyed, retrospectively, your experiences to see what indications there may have been, if any, of a "master plan" for expulsion of the population.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your opinion at the end of it was?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion was that up until the moment that we drove out of Kosovo on the 20th of March, I came across no indications that there was a plan to expel the civilian population. I was absolutely clear that there was a plan to deal with the Kosovo Liberation Army, which would involve bringing in reinforcements of the Yugoslav army, and those reinforcements had started to arrive before we -- before we left. But I was not -- I saw no evidence myself that such a plan to expel the civilian population existed as at the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to flesh that out a little bit, you, I think, take the view that bus and train transport could be organised at short notice. That was your --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And when, a little time later, the Pristina was emptied of its inhabitants forcibly, using the train, this involved simply using one train that went backwards and forwards from Pristina to the border with as many carriages on it as could be put on it. Now, even in England, that could be done quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think another point you had in mind -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the reason I stopped, General, was because of the translation problem. And if you keep picking up because you think I'm waiting for you, we'll never get anywhere. It's not your fault, it's mine. If I can just finish my question and then you can add what you want to say to the answer. I think another point that you had in mind is that the first reports of mass killings that you received via sat phones, there was no indication of pre-planning in those that you were able to see at the distance.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We remained in contact. The liaison officers who had been assigned to work with the KLA remained in contact with them when we evacuated, and it was via them that we got the first contacts, the first reports, which were on -- in the course of the 24th of March, by which stage, of course, we were in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 228. Another matter. Of course, the Chamber will in due course hear other evidence about these topics, but your view at the time, I think, as to refugee flows and how the figures compared with UNHCR was what -- with the figures provided by UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNHCR made a number of statements along the lines of, As a result of actions, 10.000 people have become refugees and internally displaced. That may have been the number that started from a place, but the -- the tendency of the villagers in the next village to take people in and give them shelter meant that it was very difficult to actually find these 10.000 people to be able to really verify that there were 10.000 people away from their homes. We certainly went out looking for them, and of course, we had a lot of people on the ground to try to find large groups of people in the hills, and we found it very difficult to find those people. So our estimates tended not to be as great as those provided by UNHCR at the time. And again, that's before the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were -- you nevertheless generally deferred to UNHCR, when it was necessary, for the conflict between impressions and statistics to be --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- resolved.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there to support each other and not to make life difficult for each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 229. You record a demeaning remark made by Kotur about Kosovar Albanians not knowing how to bury or honour their own dead.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of certainly two remarks that I recall Kotur making to me in the course of a day that we spent going around the border zone. On coming out of an Albanian village, we went past the -- their cemetery, which was set in a copse of trees, and he said, "Look. Look at this, they don't even bury their dead properly." And a few minutes later, he said, "You have to understand that these are very primitive people," which I told him that I profoundly disagreed with. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that -- let me interrupt you there. Was there an attitude that was unique to Kotur or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that that was an opinion that was shared by the people that I dealt with in the -- in the Yugoslav establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to the next exhibit, 43. Tab 43, OTP reference 2802, paragraph 230. Now, this document, which is an English document from the OSCE by Ciaglinski, provides reports on deployments along the border with Albania. And its significance?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was produced while the Rambouillet negotiations were under way and was as a result of a request from Rambouillet to get -- give an opinion from the ground on what the security situation was and might be on the border between Kosovo and Albania, the point being that, at that stage of the Rambouillet negotiations, there was talk of withdrawing Yugoslav police and security forces from inside Kosovo except within the border security zone since that was -- that was allowed for at that stage of the Rambouillet negotiations. And a figure, a strength figure for the forces that would be allowed in that zone had been postulated. As a result of my experience on the border with Colonel Kotur earlier and an appreciation we had done in the KVM and subsequent discussions with both Colonel Kotur and with General Loncar, we put this together, which really laid out what we saw the facts to be and the sort of strength that we felt would be needed in order to make this border secure, having allowance for the fact that the Yugoslav army did not have night vision devices, intruder alarms, and all the other modern stuff that -- that is available elsewhere. And the conclusion was that you needed a lot of people, which wasn't -- wasn't -- the number we came to was actually quite a lot bigger than the number that was being discussed at Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. See if we can deal with a few paragraphs by some yes/no questions to save some time. 231 was an area in Glogovac and I think an area at a battery factory in Mitrovica, to the first of which the KVM were never given access and about which you both had -- about both of which you had suspicions that they may have been covert paramilitary bases.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We attempted to get into them and were not able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next, 223. I think you've covered -- sorry, 233. You've really covered your developing state of mind about the chains of command for the MUP and the VJ being separate or connected, and nothing you need to add to that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although at 234, you make the point that the chains of command were "more closely linked than we thought..." Was that the incident at Rogovo, and how do you connect that with what you saw at Racak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Racak, it dawned on me that if you are going to put policemen in -- into the village as -- on foot or in vehicles while they are being covered by Yugoslav army who are manning the heavy weapons on the -- on the hills, there must be a very, very tight degree of coordination between those two -- the people who are running those two activities. And I realised that you could only do that if -- if there was, at the very least, a joint command post where radios -- radio nets out to the police and radio nets out to the army units were all coming in to one place. It simply could not be done otherwise without a very grave risk of hitting your own people. A blue-on-blue engagement, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You also included in your reasoning, so far as Rogovo is concerned, that Loncar was in the police chain of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The policemen at Rogovo, two weeks after Racak, were reporting to Loncar and asking him for instructions, and he was giving instructions and they were going off and getting on with them. I say this not by knowing the language but by watching what was going on, and it's quite clear when someone goes up to someone and asks for instructions and is given instructions by a superior and goes off to do them. It's not -- you don't face each other and talk in a way that you do when you're having a conversation. There was an air of command about Loncar when he was -- when he was at Rogovo that was the same with the military and with the police people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something - paragraph 240 - reflected also in the hostage-taking negotiations.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Again, there were moments when I spoke to Loncar over the phone and was able to get an answer straight away rather than him saying, "Well, I'll have to get back to you." He was able to say, "Yes, we'll do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 241. You explain how in the first few weeks of February 1999, the VJ and the MUP were responding much as they had done in December and January, but then you say that, from the middle of January, they regularly left a foot on the ground, and as time went by -- by which you mean a platoon-sized foot. And as time went by, your assessment was that by the 3rd of March they had the equivalent of how many companies?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that stage, they had the equivalent of 15 companies, by which we meant about 2.000 men deployed outside barracks against what had been the agreement of 400, or three companies. So it's a factor of five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some exhibits that we'll try to deal with swiftly: Paragraph 242, tab 44, a letter from you to General Loncar, alerting him. The first paragraph says it has come to your attention a significant amount of looting of private homes being done, followed by some specific examples being set out.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a follow-up to an earlier discussion I had had with General Loncar when I brought it to his attention that we were seeing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. signs of looting, and he said, "Well, I must have specific instances." And so I said, "Right, I'll get you some," and this was the result of it. And as you can see, they are specific places and specific times, and therefore, it should have been perfectly possible to know which units were there, but we at no stage received any follow-up to that, no explanation was offered, and to the best of my knowledge, no disciplinary action or instructions were -- were ever taken forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think in March the KVM became aware of an extension of the conscript service period. Its result, of course, in arithmetic terms, is obvious if those conscripted stayed in Kosovo rather than being deployed anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was always the understanding that there would be rotation of conscripts, that the ones who had served the full period of their conscript service would be released and the new intake of conscripts would be taken on and, by that means, the overall numbers would remain the same. So in order to take on your new conscripts but retain your old ones, obviously the number goes up by several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 45, OTP reference 2697. On this occasion, if the Court's papers are the same as mine, we have the declaration of where it was found at the first page. His Honour Judge Kwon's questions of yesterday are well in hand. I'm waiting for a translation of a piece of paper to deal with the problems of those documents most satisfactorily, but let's deal with this tab 45. This document is a routine order, I think, dated the 15th of March, or a special routine order.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5th, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 5th of March. A document you hadn't seen until recently, I think.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you tell us about it, please.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- can we go to the next page of it -- is a special routine order to the units of the Pristina Corps which are engaged on boarder security duties, issued under the signature block of the corps commander, which as has been said, I have not seen before March 2002. But it states, and let us try to find where it states it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's, I think, at the end of the second paragraph, isn't it, "If the --"

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- situation so requires."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's that there. Down a bit. Down a bit. No. No, sorry. No, that way, I think. Yes. That if the military and security situation so requires, the PRK, which is the Pristina Corps, will receive reinforcements and execute every task placed before it. That statement that the Pristina Corps would receive reinforcements indicates an intention to breach the Naumann-Clark agreement of the 25th of October, 1998, in which it was stated that the force levels would return to their February 1998 levels and -- and would remain there. And so at this stage, which is two weeks before -- before we evacuate, the corps commander is already stating to his soldiers that they are ready to bring in extra troops, which I think firmly indicates that there was a plan to -- to reinforce heavily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we move to the end of the next paragraph, where the business of the extension of military service -- I think it was by 30 days, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the time, yes. It's stated that the reasons for extending the period of military service, which applied to last March's intake of conscripts, had been understood as right and were accepted. That was clearly the corps commander's view; it may have not been the view of every conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, did the KVM then become aware of an additional unit coming into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of March, the KVM reported that a unit equipped with a different tank, a T72 tank, had arrived in Kosovo by rail. This was quite easy to notice in that every tank unit in Kosovo until that point had been equipped with the T55, which is a very different tank and just looks different in the way that -- you know, its profile is different and it's quite easy to see. It's one of the things that we spent a lot of time learning when we were young. And in fact, the man that saw it, actually saw them arriving was Richard Ciaglinski. So he can add to this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 46 we can pass over because it is in fact duplicative of the tab two tabs before, I think.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 47, tab 47. If we go to that. And again, if the usher would be good enough to just briefly lay the original version on the overhead projector, the display, before turning to the English version. This is an attack order dated mid-February, 13th of February, when the Rambouillet talks were under way, I think. Your comment on it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had not seen this before a month ago, but this is a -- or this appears to be a Yugoslav military operation order dated mid-February, that is, while the Rambouillet talks were ongoing, indicating that the FRY forces were still initiating offensive action in the area around Mitrovica. And if you can see, with some of the forces, a company of the Kosovska Mitrovica PJP will break up the terrorist forces in a dynamic operation on the following axis and subsequently continue actions in the Bajgora village Kovacevic-Gornja Lapastica axis. This is a wide area. This is not moving against a small, you know, one location because you've got good intelligence. This is an area certainly 20 kilometres by 20 kilometres. And so this indicates a search-and-destroy sort of approach to terrorism rather than the focused move against specific targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 has its own characteristic feature to it, I think. The unit members are forbidden --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's further down, isn't it. At the bottom, yes. Engage security organs principally in the counter-intelligence protection of units, inspection of security measures ... preventing theft and looting of property and checking out the territory. So it appears that there were orders given to prevent and provide against any looting of property, but I was not aware that this order was being given because it was certainly not reflective of the situation that we saw on the ground where buildings continued to be looted by the security forces after they had been secured by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The attempt -- the order to keep out the media, which we can find as well --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- entering the zone of combat operations, how does that fit with the agreement that you'd had?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I -- sorry. Can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same page, 4, just above 7.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm lost. Yes, got it. It's there. Yes. Here we have the order to prevent any attempt by the media, by humanitarian or other organisations to enter the zone of combat operations and, to this end, to engage MUP points -- at checkpoints. By this, I read that the police forces were to be used to put out checkpoints which would prevent both the media and ourselves from entering the zone of combat operations, and that, as far as it relates to the KVM, was a clear breach of the agreement which allowed us complete freedom of movement throughout Kosovo in order to verify what was going on. So by this stage, there had clearly been a conscious decision to bar us from the areas where combat operations were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Move to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you make comments on the second paragraph of the same page too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one that says, "During support, withdraw the civilian population from the zone of combat operations, making sure that terrorists do not use them as shields during the withdrawal"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that I did not see any attempt, nor did I ever hear of any attempt to withdraw the civilian population so as to protect them. Rather the opposite, if anything. I saw very little attempt to segregate those that were fighters and those that were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke from time to time yesterday about how attitudes of KVM were softened by experience so that what at one stage would have been described as a serious situation rapidly became described as a normal or quiet day because your tolerance, as it were, had changed, your tolerance level had changed. And I think tab 48, which we can deal with I hope perhaps briefly, is a similar example of that, is it not? It's a Prizren report for the 15th of February, which we can see on the first page, under the summary, describes a quiet day?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a quiet day with limited activities of MUP, VJ and KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When one looks at the content of the document - and we needn't go into it detail - by earlier standards, would it have been anything like a quiet day?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this would have been an exceptional day certainly in late November, early December, or even in early January, I think. This would have been seen as a peak of violence. And so we certainly had been desensitised by this stage, and the word "quiet" certainly in February did not mean what "quiet" meant in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 49, the daily report for the 20th/21st of February. Rambouillet talks still running. And we now see, I think -- find the passage, "Verifiers being assaulted by police officers," and your conclusion, from what you read here?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that the attitude to the KVM by the -- by the VJ and the MUP had changed and appeared to have changed officially. Specifically, we had two verifiers assaulted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page, please, Usher, to page -- the second page, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see -- yes. A serious assault occurred by police officers, that is, by Serbian police officers, against two international staff in the area south of Pristina on the 21st of February. And this was a situation where a vehicle was sitting by the roadside, watching what was going on. Policemen got out of a vehicle, went up to the verifiers, one put on a balaclava to -- so that he could not be identified, and a weapon was pointed at my verifiers, and the verifiers were then physically assaulted. And this was, I believe, the first time that this had actually happened. It was certainly the first time that it had happened by policemen in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 50. OTP reference 1696. A daily report. Your comment on this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This deals with an incident south-east of Mitrovica at which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first page, I think at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at Mitrovica, the -- there had been a murder in a village which -- in which both Serbs and Kosovar Albanians lived. This appeared to have started as a domestic dispute but became -- became more serious. The KLA became involved. The Serbian security forces became involved. And in the middle of it, the firing died down and the media went forward to interview various people and the firing started up again, which meant that we then had a firefight with the media in a -- taking cover in a puddle in the middle of the firefight. And that then took us about two hours to calm everybody down and extract the media, one member of whom was actually wounded slightly. But the -- I think the real implication of it was that this was another incident in the middle of the Rambouillet negotiations where neither side was exercising restraint. Both were allowing themselves to be drawn into these encounter -- these encounter incidents, and nobody was trying to -- neither side was trying to damp them down because of the importance the negotiations going on at Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 51, OTP reference 1697, just for completeness, and I don't think you want to add any comments about it, but this is the -- if we look at the original on the overhead projector briefly, this is the MUP report of the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. It's the -- it's just the other side, the other version of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's there for completeness.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can then move on to tab 52. We've now reached the end of Rambouillet. 26th of February. And this document, from yourselves, draws attention, on the first page, to harassment of 13. We can see it under 1B, internationals and eight locals detained at the border of Macedonia by the FRY authorities. How was this viewed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was seen as an extremely serious breach of the diplomatic status of the -- of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Every time a vehicle crossed the border into -- into FYROM, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, there was generally delay and there was generally invitation to open the vehicle to search which was always refused because of the diplomatic status. In this instance, the first vehicle to arrive was asked to open the -- the rear of the vehicle for inspection. He declined and, at that point, every vehicle that arrived was similarly detained and the situation became quite threatening; and in the end, the only way that the situation was resolved was by the Head of Mission going down to the border and personally opening the boot of the vehicle in order to secure the release of his verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 53. 2804 OTP reference. Really I think a document -- I don't know that there's anything you particularly want to draw from it save to say that it is a reflective account of matters at the time and it's here for completeness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document of reference for your evidence. Tab 54, OTP reference 2805, is a record of a 10th of March meeting. Your comment on it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again this is a document which shows the sort of thinking we were doing at the time. It's talking about the possibility of a fracture within the KLA structure, which was clearly of interest to us at the time. And it is one of the documents which was produced from -- from one of the liaison officers who dealt permanently with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 256 in your document. There were some operations in this period at Kacanik and Vucitrn about which you formed certain views, I think.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two areas that were concerned were two separate brigade areas, and so it was my assessment that this must have been an operation that was planned at above the local level and therefore at least at the corps level from Pristina. By this stage there was a definite -- there was a definite feeling that there were ongoing -- there was an ongoing offensive attitude by the VJ and the MUP in the way that they were conducting the -- their operations. They had a set procedure whereby the area would be sealed off by the police, who would put up checkpoints at all -- at all places where roads entered an area, and then the VJ and the MUP combined would then sweep the area inside the cordon. It was, therefore, difficult to get inside that cordon, although we did on occasions, and we were more forced to rely on the columns of smoke one could see coming from the villages where the operation was going on than being able in every case to get to the village and to report what was happening first hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the size of units you can help us with.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I certainly saw myself on at least one occasion, and this was reflected by reports of others to me, was that there were at least -- at least one and probably two company-sized units, that is, units of about 120 to 150 strong, of police which looked quite different to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. average police that we had been dealing with. They looked fitter. They carried themselves more proudly. They -- their morale seemed to be much higher than the police units we had come across to date, obviously with the exception of the police at Rogovo that I've talked about earlier. These people at the time had very modern equipment, and webbing equipment as opposed to the rather battered stuff that some of the others had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 55. Briefly to indicate the circumstances about the 19th of February, under destabilisation. We see that you were having to face, according to intelligence passed to you, the possibility of the assassination of Walker or hostage-taking.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was information which I was given which I then brought up with -- with the Serb authorities, seeking to get from them an assurance that this was -- was not the case. I have to say that I got some assurances but not -- not complete ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This intelligence included, as a possibility, the wearing of the other side's uniforms by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a persistent concern to us. Each -- at each incident, the possibility that -- that the uniforms of the other side were being used was always present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 258. On the 25th of February, you became aware of the KLA attempt to open a new zone of operations away from its former centres of interest, this time in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area in the very south of Kosovo which has got the pass going through it from -- from the rest of Kosovo down to Macedonia and was the main route out for -- if we were going to evacuate, it was the one we used so it was of great concern to us. The KLA made an appearance in this area, and there was, very quickly, a VJ counterattack which was actually successful and which secured the high ground on either side of the road that was going through it. Once that had been done, the road was then picketed with a number of -- of VJ units at the key points along it, including the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 56. An OSCE report of the 12th of March noting in the italicised passage on the first page no willingness of parties to de-escalate their military posture and clashes between the KLA and Serb security forces. And I think we can find reference to what you've just told us of the KLA stepping up their activities in Kacanik which led to the displacement of -- this is on the second page, in the third paragraph -- to the displacement of some 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was prepared for the Chairman-in-Office of the OSCE for him to send to the United Nations, because he felt the situation was deteriorating so gravely and so quickly that this needed to be brought to the formal attention of the United Nations. You can see at the bottom of that third paragraph on page 2, an estimated 2.000 people had fled villages in the Kacanik area with some trying to cross the border to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. And that estimated 2.000 was our conservative estimate rather than anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see, of course, reference further down the page to a Serbian restaurant in Pec with injuries and then seven Albanians later killed. I mean, seven people, sorry, wounded, and one of them died, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And again this is another very, very serious day in which this had -- this was only just more than the normal level of violence by this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The time means that we probably shouldn't linger on it. In fact, at page 5 I think you can find reference to the detention of OSCE vehicles on the 25th and 26th of February --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- contrary, as asserted, to the Vienna Convention on diplomatic --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- immunities. Right. Paragraph 262. You've made an earlier reference to what hadn't been done to bridges by the KLA, but in February, you started noticing things that were being done to bridges, this time by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bridges specifically in the Kacanik D file and specifically one large bridge and two tunnels were prepared for demolition in this period. Now, in order to do this, you have to put out a cable, which is time-consuming, all around the bridge so that the electric current can be -- can reach all of the explosives, and then at a later stage -- later state, you then attach the explosives. Both are time-consuming things, and, therefore, if you are going to adopt an increased alert, this is one of the things that traditionally you do. And it was certainly an indication to us that the level of preparedness of the VJ in this area had been increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What could have been the military objective? Just explain for those who have no experience of these things.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road from Kacanik down to -- down to Macedonia was obviously also the road from Macedonia up to Kacanik. And so, with NATO sitting in Macedonia in some force, if they were going to move into Kosovo, this was the logical and really the only feasible route in for heavy armoured vehicles at that time of the year. And so if that bridge had been blown, it would have been very much more difficult for such an entry to have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 57. A weekly summary by the data fusion cell of the KVM for the 26th of February to the 4th of March. Now, it deals with a number of topics, and we certainly won't go through it in detail. As to the MUP, and I think this will be on the second page, or starting on the second page, you deal with the preparations for demolition at the foot of the page -- or not you --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The authors have dealt with that at the foot of the page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Which says: "A number of bridges, tunnels and culverts have been prepared for demolition on routes into and from Albania and Macedonia. The forces around the bridge demolition on the road from Djeneral Jankovic have been notably increased, possibly a reflection on the KLA security nearby." I certainly personally saw that and, having been trained as an engineer, I do know what preparing a bridge for demolition and preparing a tunnel for demolition looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's also a reference, if we can find it, to combat teams in excess of numbers being deployed and MUP patrolling in Orahovac and Suva Reka. If you can't find it immediately --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've got it. "VJ forces within Kosovo have significantly increased their training and deployments throughout the province. Although there are significantly more VJ troops out of barracks than there have been since October, an estimated 15 combat teams deployed, their actions have been somewhat low key in light of what can only be described as KLA provocation. There's been a build-up of VJ forces on the periphery of Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say of the KVM that, even at this 11th hour, KVM was punctilious in its objective reporting.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our words in the conclusion, saying, "In response to this, the Serbs have held back to a degree" does indicate the fact that we were still attempting to report what we saw as -- as dispassionately as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 264. I'm just going to deal with that, if I can, by a yes-or-no question. Apart from the incident of the man or the men in grey overalls or uniforms at Rogovo, it was difficult for you to gauge the build-up of MUP forces because they weren't confined to barracks and were operating in smaller groups, and you proposed to Loncar a regime for monitoring MUP rotations be established, and he rejected that idea.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 58, memorandum from the OSCE of the 16th of March dealing with visits to MUP police stations in Eastern Kosovo. Now, it speaks here of stations above the baseline. In the middle of the page. And it suggests, I think, that three more police stations need to be identified and these name various. The significance of this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is that while you could not do a formal head count on the MUP, you could obviously count where the police stations were. And so to find three extra police stations popping up was, at the very least, an indication that there were more police, and certainly it was indicated more locations from which police were operating. Again, this is information which should have been routinely communicated to the OSCE and which was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 59. A fragmentary order. Tell us what "FRAGO" means.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A full operation order is normally many pages long, and so if you just want to get one message out, you send out a fragmentary order, which is abbreviated as a FRAGO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The figures of this one?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was talking about the VJ and MUP reinforcements arriving in the area in the west of Kosovo and telling everyone to be on the alert for any other movement within their area. It was really a reminder to everyone to report everything that was happening at a time when there was quite a lot of movement going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the date of this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 12th of March, which is a week before we evacuated. And so obviously there was quite a high level of activity going on at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we've got this curious entry on the right-hand side, just above the word "FRAGO." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. The 21st of June, 00, is, I think, the moment at which this was printed from the disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the copy, for production purposes.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another detail that you deal with in your document at broadly the same time. We'll just deal with it here. You were aware of a change in KLA leadership. First of all, where did you get that intelligence or information from, if you can help us? And then tell us what the effect of it was as you understood it.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information came to me from the liaison officers that we had got on a permanent basis, co-located with the KLA and dealing with them on a daily basis. It would have been a combination of formal reporting and verbal reporting. Sometimes when things were particularly sensitive, it always didn't get committed to paper, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the nature of the change?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of the change was that we understood that all of the -- I was going to say moderate but I would say less hard-line members of the KLA were being replaced by people who were more uncompromising, and this was as Rambouillet was drawing to a close so it clearly had grave implications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 60, report of the 2nd of March. We can go to the second page of it for the Pec district.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's page 2. Top of it, I think, Pec. There. In this, the chief of police -- the situation was tense in the area of VJ hill, which was a nickname of a location, as a result of a joint police -- army and police exercise by a reinforced tank company. The chief of police in Pec denied police involvement while the army representatives confirmed it. This indicated to us that there was an increasing level of inter-operation between the VJ, the army, and the police, which contrasts with the situation at the start of the mission, as I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, the Court will have noticed that the quotation of the document in paragraph 269 is in error in the second use of the word "denied." It should be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've dealt with this before and there's perhaps only one outstanding question to be asked, and that is: If there were joint commands, did you ever locate a joint command centre?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as such, but the proximity of the police and the army headquarters in Pristina was such that it could easily have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us these were buildings to which you were not given access.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And they faced each other across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 61. A report. Again original, please, briefly to the overhead projector so that we can see the original in -- briefly. Thank you very much. And then we'll place the English translation on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, this is a reported response by the VJ or MUP to a KLA attack on the 20th of March, a document you hadn't seen until recently.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On reading it, its significant to you being what?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, it's the response by the VJ and MUP to a KLA attack. It describes casualties in the MUP and the VJ, and indicates that this response to the original attack by the KLA was again a combined VJ and MUP operation. It's also significant in describing a policeman injuring himself with a negligent discharge from his own weapon. And I would point out that this indicates a poor standard of training in weapon handling that you would not expect in police forces which are dealing with terrorism and are attempting to portray themselves as being a professional force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with 273 and 274 perhaps by some questions susceptible to yes/no answers to save time. I think you've dealt already with Loncar's apparent links to Belgrade and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He being able to give rapid answers to questions about VJ dispositions.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And likewise, when you needed decisions about KLA leaders being taken to Pristina airport for Rambouillet, Loncar was able to facilitate that very quickly --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- which led you to the conclusion that he was linked to Belgrade with executive authority over some aspects of security forces.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And over the VJ negotiations which you've told us about, one particular aspect that was significant was when a proposal was put to Sainovic by Keller, you received an answer very rapidly but you received it from --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Loncar. And I got the impression that if they were not sitting in the same room, they were certainly talking at very, very regular intervals by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, according to your colleague Pellnas, Sainovic had actually said something about delegated authority being given to Loncar.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was over the issue of the helicopter, which we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So at paragraph 275; although Sainovic was regularly presented to you as the man with authority, or people did do that, was there ever any issue as to his constitutional position?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everyone accepted that he was the man who had to be dealt with in -- over these issues. And significantly, we never ever heard the name Andjelkovic mentioned, who you'll recall was the leader of the Temporary Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there was another example, in a sense, not of the gravest kind, where Ambassador Walker was accosted by drunken policemen and had to complain about it, raise the issue with Sainovic, who appeared to be aware of the incident already and said he'd deal with it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not in any way surprised by it and did not in fact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question the facts, which was often the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out on these topics at 278, as you've already told us yesterday, I think, Kotur's views on one or two things and one or two individuals, but I think that may be a matter of detail into which I needn't descend.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please, just a few exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's 10.15. This being a suitable moment, we'll adjourn for quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 62, please, General. It's a Security Council Resolution, and it's included here. We can deal with it briefly. It demands the complete and verifiable phase withdrawal from Kosovo of military police and paramilitary forces. Do you have any comment on this or its timing?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was dated the 10th of June, which was the authority to enter Kosovo. And of course, we entered Kosovo with the UN forces and with the NATO forces, starting on the 12th of June, and this was the authority for the deployment into Kosovo specifically of the UN mission to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the meantime, the only information coming to you being bits and pieces, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I personally stayed in Macedonia until late April of 1999, when I then went back to the UK. And I returned to Macedonia on the -- on Friday, the 11th of June, and went into Kosovo with -- with KFOR on -- on the first day, as an extra liaison officer with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of things about what you found in Pristina, in the main police headquarters there, paragraph 282.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day in Kosovo, people only went in in -- the advance elements went in, and I actually arrived in Kosovo, with a vehicle, on a permanent basis the next day, which was Sunday, I think, the 13th of June. At that point, there were a number of people taking up residence within the police headquarters which was rapidly emptying, and in the course of that, torture instruments were located in the basement and the cells of the main police headquarters in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Torture instruments" is a somewhat dramatic phrase and can cover a range of things from medieval times to the modern, so I think we better be a bit specific.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were certainly sticks, clubs, and electric wires that were capable of being attached to parts of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the subject of wires, did you see rather more substantial wires in the form of cables?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of IT and communications cables which were running from the Pristina Corps headquarters building into the basement of the Grand Hotel, and it was in the basement of the Grand Hotel that I had the first meetings with the VJ officers to discuss the phase -- lines for the phased withdrawal of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without beating about the bush, this cabling being consistent with, if no more than that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly being capable of moving a lot of information. Whether it was monitoring what was going on in the hotel or allowing operations that would normally have taken place in the Pristina Corps headquarters to be -- to take place from the basement of the Grand Hotel to protect them from air raids, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we look at the last half dozen or so exhibits, just two general comments on topics you haven't covered, one of them I think not in the statement, at least not collected in the statement at any paragraph. Paramilitaries. In the course of your time there, what if any observations did you make about paramilitary groups on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly appeared to be able to -- they were able to appear quite quickly at will throughout the area, and it was my impression that they were not always coming from outside of Kosovo for specific events. Therefore, it was likely that there was an area from which they were operating within, within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you've already told us of a couple of --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I think. Were you able to see any pattern in events that could indicate how they were controlled or managed or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly how many occasions and how many different types of paramilitaries did you identify, if you can be specific at all?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the -- the one specific moment when I myself confronted them was when we -- we had the roadblocks in early January, but there were other occasions which indicated that there was activity going on at a fairly regular level, particularly the very constant level of people being killed in the night and their bodies dumped. Whether it was Albanians who were said to be loyal to Serbs or Serbs who might have been friendly with Albanians, but there was a trickle of about four killings per week throughout the period that just went on and were never cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But of course, you -- you're not in any position, as I understand your answer, specifically to connect them to paramilitaries or to any particular paramilitaries. It's simply a matter of inference, is that it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my inference, and it certainly is in keeping with the pattern that has been observed in other insurgent campaigns, that paramilitaries exist and do these extrajudicial killings of people who they see as a threat or are informers or anything else that offends them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Then turning to the other side now, on paragraph 283; you have summarised there your anecdotal analysis of the KLA types. Really in just a couple of sentences if you could boil down 283 for us.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say there were all sorts within the KLA. Certainly there was an element of criminality in -- in some of the people. In others, they seemed to be people who had taken up arms for more ideological reasons; and the degree of control that was exercised also varied tremendously. There were some commanders who we felt, if we went to them and said, "Can you do such-and-such," and they said, "Yes," they would do it. There were others who would say, "Well, maybe," and then would say, "Well, it's very difficult to control my people." And so there was a very wide spectrum from people who were on the verge of criminality or involved in criminality to people who genuinely felt that they were living with a repressive regime that needed to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think - for a couple of yes-or-no answers - that you thought the criminal element, if there was one, in the KLA, entirely anecdotally, increased the closer you got to Pec; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That was certainly our feeling, that in dealing with the commanders in that area, they were among the ones who were most difficult to get agreement with and get them to stick to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you also concluded that there seemed to be quite a degree of local autonomy given to local commanders.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They all had the right of doing anything they felt they needed to do if they felt they were in danger, which is a pretty broad spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So whereas, for example, at the time of the release of the prisoners, the eight VJ soldiers, KLA high command would give assurances. Those assurances might be more difficult of delivery by those further down the chain than would have first been presented.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few remaining documents, then, please. Tab 63, OTP reference 2808, which is simply a chronology of events, and it's really a document of record for us and for the Chamber should we find it helpful to refer to it. I don't think we need refer to it otherwise. It's a chronology that you've produced of OSCE events.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Which I wrote on the 4th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see it and we can simply turn to it if and when we find it helpful. To save time, we'll simply note that it's there. Sixty-four, tab 64, which is a memorandum, I think key points from a meeting on the 29th of December?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've referred to this earlier, but it is a meeting which took place in my absence, which is why -- which is why Maisonneuve was there in my place. But it also had Ciaglinski there, so you might want to invite him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- with Ciaglinski when he comes. I think it will be next week. Sixty-five, OTP 2810, is a summary, and between pages 4 and 10, I think, or contains between 4 and 10 a record of non-compliance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And this is another of the periodic documents we put together for the Chairman-in-Office in Vienna, putting everything into one document rather than letting them produce their own summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we simply lay on the overhead projector the first page because it will do as a representative page.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one. It's the one after this. Sorry, we're one document behind at the moment. Yes, that's it. Get to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another document we have, and here we can see on the 20th of January, the MUP surrounding two houses suspected of harbouring KLA, ceasefire arranged, a fire with small arms, MUP firing on the houses, killing two men inside. And then the columns on the right-hand side set the non-compliance by reference to the paragraph numbers of the document that we've been looking at right from the beginning of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then 66. I don't know if -- this is a record of a phone call you made with General Loncar. The significance?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the lead-up to the start of the early attempts to go and verify units in their barracks, and the gist of it was that Loncar was saying, "Can you please delay everything, because everything will be sorted out at the meeting between Walker and Sainovic," which, remember, was not actually the case, but that was what this telephone conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sixty-seven. OTP reference 2812. 23rd of December, 1998, so we've gone back in time. Meeting with Colonel Marinkovic. Significance of this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the first units had -- unit had come out of barracks and had gone to a -- the airfield south of Podujevo, and having gone there, we went to the unit and asked to see the commanding officer to talk to him about what precisely he thought he was doing out of barracks when there was an agreement that such action would not take place. And so it was the start of the series of events that led to increasing numbers of VJ being out of barracks. And again, it's a record that was made at the time on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sixty-eight. It has a declaration as to a chain of custody or provenance, and then on -- so the original should be placed briefly on the overhead projector before we look at the English version of it. It's OTP reference 1320.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This outlines the security situation as at late September 1998. So it reflects a time when I was not present. But at this point, the assessment is that the VJ and MUP feel that they've gained the upper hand over the UCK, and significantly, perhaps, that they detected a UCK or a KLA presence in the Kacanik area in the south; and certainly by the time we got there, we did not feel there was such a presence later in the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go to the next exhibit, 69, OTP 2686. This document doesn't have a declaration as to where it's been found. That will have to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. There's a matter I want to raise with this general. I just wonder if you could help with something, General. If you go back to 68. I just want your assistance in interpreting the document. The main paragraph. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you just look at the main paragraph - it needn't be put on the ELMO - in the middle of the document. It talks about the security situation in the territory remains complex, and it's worst on the -- and it gives a number of -- the names of a number of villages, and it says on an axis. Then it goes on: "In the event of any action by the VJ and MUP on the --" and then two more village names, the village line "-- the main part of the terrorism should be expected along the line." Does that mean, as you understand it, literally a line or is it a reference to an area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does it mean? I've seen it in another orders. It's puzzled me as to what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Along a line," I would interpret, sir, as being the area that you can expect to find them. Clearly, when you're in an insurgency situation, you've got a fairly good idea about where you can expect to run into the insurgents and where the security situation is less tense, and it's -- it's of -- of interest to security forces, because they will have maps on which they've got blobs of different colours, saying, "When you go into this area, no vehicles on their own, always two vehicles, always have a radio, always have weapons with you," whereas outside that area, the situation may well be much more benign. We certainly drew similar circles on the maps of the areas where we knew we could confidently expect the KLA to be and areas where they might be seen and they might operate on an infrequent basis. And so to define an area as a "line" is not a precise thing, but it gives a commander who is going to go into this area the idea of south of a certain point you would, for instance, load your weapons. You would adopt a different state of alertness. You might put your steel helmets on and take your berets off. And so all of those things will come from this sort of statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sixty-nine, tab 69, 2686 document, the source of which will have to be dealt with in an addendum to the exhibit volume, but if we look at the original just briefly to see what it is, on the overhead projector, and then at the translation.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report which is from the MUP and which describes the fact that two of the policemen who are clearly on detached duty in Kosovo have decided they've had enough and they want to go home, and this is dated the 20th of November. And so it is clear that there were morale problems within the security forces as early as the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 70. I think one of our documentary reports, OTP 1563, and it's simply only of value in case we want to discover what the manpower position was of the KVM as at the 2nd of January.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And defines it as 492. Around 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Seventy-one and two -- 71 was photographs. 72 was a document you hadn't had a chance to review before Easter. Again it's a document the source of which will have to be covered in a supplementary piece of paper, but I think you may have had about 30 seconds to look at it yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is the document which -- whose translation is the Yugoslav Army General Staff, a military secret internal, a memorandum for Yugoslav army members engaged in territory affected by terrorist sabotage raids, and dated June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're short a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one copy or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Later will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This deals with the proper way of handling certain circumstances, General, and your brief observation on it would be what?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can take you to the last page of the document which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. says what has to be done with this document. And it says that this memorandum shall be sent to units at company and independent platoon level. In other words, down to every group of around 40 or 50 men engaged in a territory where there's a possibility of terrorist sabotage raids, get through the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Speed when reading, General.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Going to the next paragraph. "Systematically go through the entire reminder with all army members on the territory where sabotage and terrorist attacks are conducted and proper individuals -- prepare individuals and units to implement the prescribed procedures." And it finishes: "Officers in command positions shall be responsible for the consistent implementation of the reminder in their formations." This, I think, indicates that there was a set of rules to be followed in dealing with the insurgents, and it is clear that instructions were transmitted down the chain of command. If we go back to the start of the document, on page 2 in the first paragraph, it says -- that's it. Yes. Sorry. This says it's the procedure to be followed by VJ members in an area under threat by -- affected by terrorist and sabotage activities. If you go down to the fourth subparagraph, they're to take rigorous measures to prevent unmilitary conduct by individuals, units and commands. So this is the instruction to the commander. If we go further down, into the area where there are bullets, bullet points, to the paragraph that starts, "While fighting outlaws and terrorists..." Yes, that's it. "When hostile groups conduct action from fortified features or an inhabited place after issuing a warning, use artillery weapons for direct targeting and selectively destroy the enemy and the features from which activity is conducted." I would be very worried about this word "selective." I think this is a very loose document. It clearly condones the idea officially that you can use artillery against villages. Now, in my view, that is a very, very dangerous document to be putting down to a young officer and not necessarily giving him much more guidance than that. I don't know what guidance he got, but it is certainly not a document that would be issued in any army that I'm -- I've ever served in. And it gives too much latitude, I think, to the man on the ground. It's very dangerous. If we go on to paragraph 3, that deals with what to do with surrendered terrorists. Yes. And it specifically, at the next paragraph, it says that he is to be arrested - which is entirely right - but then at -- further down, we go down to a list of what it's forbidden to do. On another one, I think. Yes. "The following is forbidden: Killing detained persons, inflicting bodily harm on them, robbing detained persons, sick and wounded, desecrating corpses, looting them," and I think on the next page, "offending human dignity, rape, and forced prostitution." So it is quite clear that the chain of command had issued orders that those people who wished to surrender should be allowed to surrender, which seems to me to be at odds with the exceptionally high kill rate of the -- of the incidents that I observed in which, if I add them up, over a hundred people were killed at a time when nine were captured and five were wounded. So over a hundred killed for less than 20 wounded is an incredible kill rate if you are seeking to take the surrender of people who give themselves up voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go on to paragraph 4, "One should endeavour to avoid the use of artillery weapons and other weapons against citizens who are not offering any resistance, against places of worship, and the like." And that, again, is what one would hope to see, but the word "endeavour," again I would draw your attention to, because I think it should be written that every effort ought to be taken to.
