"Endeavour," is, frankly, weak in this sort of context, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe before allowing the point to fade, if we're allowed to do that, we could place the original, which is in Cyrillic, at paragraph 4. I don't know if we're allowed to do this. I've forgotten. And ask -- the witness won't be able to read it, but if the first line is susceptible to being read by the interpreters in the booth, if that's allowed, we will get an immediate translation of what's been written there. This is a draft translation. Are we allowed to do that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you're allowed to do it; whether it can be done is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If seems to me -- since emphasis is being placed on a word, I'd be unhappy about coming back months later when the point's been forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only way it can be done is if it's put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, if it can be -- it has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it on the ELMO now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is. It's the first line of the paragraph there. If the interpreters are able to read it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can the interpreters read the first line? Is it following the figure 4, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's the paragraph immediately below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The paragraph underneath the figure 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please interpret that for us, if they can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "During the execution of combat operations against sabotage terrorist groups, seek to avoid the use of artillery weapons and weapons against citizens who do not put up any resistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough, is it? "Seek" seems to be the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I return to another bit of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is in paragraph 5 -- sorry. Below the paragraph we've just done, in the next paragraph -- yes, that one. Can we... And this says that when citizens participate together with terrorist sabotage group members in armed action and offer them accommodation and food and supply them with weapons and ammunition, in such a case, they are all to be considered terrorist sabotage group members and are to be treated in the same way as terrorist sabotage group members. I think that's an extremely dangerous statement to be issued by a General Staff. It would certainly cause any lawyer, any military lawyer that I have ever met, to -- to want to talk to the commander very seriously, because it's clearly giving a lot of licence to the people on the ground to deal with someone whose house happens to have been occupied for terrorist purposes suddenly becomes a terrorist in the same breath. And in the paragraph below, again if the school, hospital, or place of worship is used by the terrorist for observation, reconnaissance, or offering armed resistance, it also is considered that it gets treated in the same way. And so this is a very, very broad catchall phrase that suggests that if someone in a terrorist group has been spotted in the area of a mosque, then that gives the green light to be able to target the mosque, which is not at all the way I would see armed forces being instructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think lastly, at 5.2. We have procedures for injured and sick saboteurs and terrorists, and that is the one -- sick and wounded, yes. And they get first aid, as they rightly should. As a comment on the whole document, I believe that, remembering where we are at this point in 1998 in the middle of the Balkans, in the light of events that had happened already between 1992 and 1999, I think this is an extremely loosely written document, and I feel it should have been far more specifically written. But even as it is written, I can think of many moments when these loose instructions were certainly flouted, and I can think of no moment when any commanding officer was, to my knowledge, actually disciplined for the breach of these very, very loose instructions, and I find that remarkable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I sit down, can I return to His Honour Judge Kwon's inquiry yesterday, which really starts with, as an example, tab 7, and provide the answer. In doing so, can I say that we will provide for insertion statements identifying the places where non-OSCE documents were found in line with the statements that have been associated with some of these exhibits coming from Mr. Milner, but number 7 was not one of those which had such an attestation. It's worth observing, and I didn't observe this yesterday, that if we look at the last page of the original of this particular document, and perhaps the witness could see this as well but he may not be able to help further with it, it's worth observing that the copying list on this document, as on many of them or all of them, I'm not sure, includes, by surname only Milosevic, Milutinovic, Milic, Sainovic, Bulatovic, Ojdanic, Ojanovic and others. That's something that is reflected elsewhere. The position about these documents is that they were seized from a house in Pristina by an investigator. I'm not going to name the householder, and confidentiality will be sought or indeed taken for that householder. The documents come in the form I'm holding them up at the moment. Tab 7 is in the one in my right hand and on your left, which is the first two of booklets. I'll hand these in, perhaps, for inspection and then we'll decide how they ought to be dealt with. The title of the two booklets concerned are as follows: Temporary Executive Council, APKIM, Conversations with Foreign Delegations, and then the one which contains tab 7 is year one, number 2, December, 1998, and the second one, which contains tabs 10, 16, 18, 28, 34 and 38 is similarly titled except that it's number 3 and January 1999. I have -- and I have for distribution copies of those two cover pages. And perhaps it would be convenient if number 2 goes in as part of tab number 7 that we've been looking at, and then the next one -- yes. I'll distribute that first to avoid confusion. So if that cover page can go in simply as part of tab 7. And then because the first of the documents that came from the second book is tab 10, if this other sheet can go in as part of tab 10. The registry's been good enough to allow us to provide the originals of the various exhibits, or the best originals that are in our possession, as it were, of the other tabs of this exhibit in due course. Can I ask that we consider the position of these books when I've handed them in, perhaps, and they've been inspected. Perhaps I -- perhaps the Judges would like to see them - I'm not sure - briefly now in light of their questions. But whether they should be exhibited now or whether they can come in as an exhibit on their own at a later stage. At the moment, they're held together by elastic bands because they had to be taken apart for the copying process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll return these and they can be decided on in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If you wait there, you'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Drewienkiewicz, your department for operations was at the top of the chain of command of the Verification Mission, was it not? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the, I think, six deputies. I was -- there was Walker, and Keller was his principal deputy, and the remaining deputies had equal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm cognisant of the explanation given by the person that you just mentioned, that is Ambassador Gabrielle Keller, who said that the department of operations had full responsibility, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered directly to -- I answered directly to the Head of Mission in many respects, because my area was fast moving. However, when Ambassador Walker was away, I answered directly to Ambassador Keller since he was in the position of Head of Mission in the absence of Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, can you explain this statement by Mr. Keller which I have quoted from his text? I'm not paraphrasing, I'm quoting him. [In English] "The officers of the KVM, supposedly a civilian operation, was successively militarised. I already mentioned the question of the chain of command. " [Interpretation] What would you say regarding the extent to which the mention was militarised and how that chain of command functioned?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at the -- there were, at the start, a lot of military officers who were made available by the sending nations to the Kosovo Verification Mission. That was largely because they were available at short notice. It is in the nature of these -- of civilian organisations that the civilians, who are often experts and specialists, have proper jobs and, therefore, cannot simply drop everything and move at no notice to a new mission. They have to give notice in their own jobs, be contacted, decide that they want to do it, make their personal arrangements. With military people, you can tell them to pack their bags and get on the aeroplane, as happened to me, within six hours. And so if a requirement comes up at very short notice, as this one did, then one of the options that the nations have is to put officers into civilian clothes and send them as unarmed people, which is what happened to us. It was certainly the intention that, as the situation was established on the ground and as the need for elections then came up, which were to be in the second half of the year that the KVM had a mandate, that the military would be reduced and that the electoral specialists would be brought in. But it would certainly have taken several months to get them, and there was great urgency and a need to get the mission effective as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I am understanding you correctly, military men were sent because it was more difficult for civilians to terminate their jobs and, to military men, you can simply issue orders. Is that the crux of what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, my question is: Is it not the same as with soldiers that are assigned by order, that you -- can't you behave similarly with diplomatic officials of an adequate rank, which all the OSCE countries have in large numbers? What is the difference between assigning military men or diplomatic officers?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference, I think, is that they are available in much larger numbers, and they are from a culture which is prepared to move quickly and to live in uncomfortable conditions, and we knew that the conditions were going to be somewhat uncomfortable, certainly at the start of the mission. Because a lot of the early work was going to be establishing locations and going out and finding out what the situation on the ground was, it was felt that, while the military people did not necessarily have all of the right diplomatic skills, their early availability and their ability to operate in difficult situations, uncomfortable situations, made them better than the alternative, which was nothing, which was a few people arriving slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the decision to send predominantly military people, was one of the reasons the nature of the assignments given to them in the mission, regardless of the way in which it was defined in the agreement Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. between the FRY and the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to send military people was a decision that was made by each individual state of the OSCE, and it varied. Some -- some states decided they would send only civilians. Some decided they would send none. And so it was -- there was no central decision by the OSCE permanent council. The only decision they made was that they wanted to build the mission up as quickly as humanly possible to its full 2.000 mandated strength. And as you see, that took quite a long time. And I have to add that one of the things I did in late December, early January, was to review where everybody was, because we knew that a number of people had been called forward from -- by Vienna to join the mission, and they didn't seem to be appearing at the right rate. And when we checked the names of those who had been called forward against those who had been -- who had arrived, we found that at the moment that we had about 500 people in the mission - we had thought we were going to have 800 - because 300 had decided that they didn't want to come. And that's the other problem with -- with dealing with people who are not subject to a military chain of command; they were able to decide that, watching the TV, it was probably not for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us make a comparison in connection with the answer you are giving. You are aware that before an agreement was reached on the Kosovo Verification Mission between Yugoslavia and the OSCE, that a Diplomatic Observer Mission was set up consisting of diplomats, diplomatic staff of the embassies which various countries had accredited in Belgrade. I assume you're aware of that, the diplomatic observation mission.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in my experience, the diplomatic observation mission consisted of one or two diplomats with quite a lot of seconded military or ex-military contracted to increase their personnel. The formal number of diplomats in the diplomatic observer missions was, in my experience, quite a small proportion. Certainly not more than 25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That in fact was the point of my question. So even the diplomatic mission was not really a diplomatic mission but a military one, according to what you have just said, because it was predominantly composed of military staff. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but its task was diplomatic. Its task was not military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In name, certainly, but would you agree with this assessment, which also comes from your colleague Ambassador Keller: [In English] "Authoritarian. Sudden decisions were taken to remove people from their positions without justification beyond an alleged incompetence. The special position --" This is the point: "... the special position of operations gave this department a prominent role with responsibilities in all fields, even outside its theoretical competence." [Interpretation] My question is, in view of the fact that you were the head of that department of operations, and as Keller says, with responsibilities in all areas even beyond theoretic competencies, would that -- does it -- can one infer from this that you were in fact the Executive Chief of Mission?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly confirm that I picked up jobs which were not being done by others, even if they were not formally part of my task, because it was important that they were done. And this was done with the agreement of the head of the mission at the time. I specifically referred earlier to the -- the problem we had over dealing with the police actions, which was not formally my side of the -- of the mission but which was simply not being done in the early days. And I took it on -- I took it on myself to do this, to expand my activities into this area because of the degree to which it was becoming clear to me and to everyone else that police and military actions were connected increasingly. I think I did become the Executive Chief of the mission, because the mission changed in its nature from being a long-term mission to one in which short-term events with an operational bias became the driving factor. And because of that, my department was in the best position to take the action that was required, and it was my department that every night got the reports from the other Regional Centres, from their heads, and we put it together for the Head of Mission. And so events moved me into that -- that position, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I had assumed. That is why I wanted to check it out. So you were, in a sense, an Executive Chief of the mission. So you had the whole mission and its activities within your responsibility. Though I must ask you now, since you just mentioned that you engaged in activities linked to the police, why did the nomination of the assistant for police affairs come late? Was it delayed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, the original nomination was not -- was not fully approved within the OSCE in Vienna, and another name was then substituted, and he arrived -- he was nominated in late December or early January and arrived in late January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The person was an Italian lawyer, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The eventual man was an Italian judge, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met the man before. I was not in Vienna when he was -- when he was in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is what was heard and what can be read in some places true, and that is that this first candidate was rejected because his position was that it was necessary to cooperate in a cordial manner with the police of Serbia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard that secondhand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And to what extent do you assume that that is true?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would -- you ought to ask that of the people that were actually in Vienna at the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you find it strange that a candidate should be rejected because he feels that one should have courteous relationships, relations of correct cooperation with the police of the country in which the mission is staying?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was everybody's intention to have courteous relationships with the police of the country in which we were. So I don't believe, as stated like that, that that would have been a cause for rejection. Everybody went out of their way to be courteous, certainly at the start, and the diplomatic formalities were well observed. So I don't believe, put in the way that you put it, that that was any cause whatsoever for anyone to be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There is an explanation here which I am again borrowing from your colleague Mr. Keller, so will you tell me whether you agree with him. He says, and I quote: [In English] "To take important decisions in the mission was the executive committee; in other words, the Head of Mission and his six deputies. In the day-to-day life of the mission, the meetings of the Executive Committee, one hour three times per week, where they wanted to handle the common business rather than making the important decisions after appropriate discussion." [Interpretation] Is this an assessment that you would agree with or does your opinion differ?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content of the meetings, which I don't recall as being three times a week, I recall as being almost every day, were to deal with the most pressing events that we were dealing with at the time. At the beginning, therefore, they dealt with the problems of building up the mission quickly, and then, as the situation deteriorated, they increasingly focused on operational matters. There were also meetings for which there was preparation about things like how we were going to start to administer the elections, the process of voter registration and this sort of thing, but they became rather overtaken by events as the situation deteriorated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is contradicted to a major extent, the further explanation. The main consequences of the above: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... some of the mission members choose from the beginning to adopt a very aggressive behaviour with the official authorities." [Interpretation] Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it depends how you define "aggressive." We were certainly determined that our freedom of movement should not be curtailed because, if it were to be curtailed, we would not be able to do our job. And so if we were aggressive at the start, it was because of our -- our wish to be as effective as possible as quickly as possible. We were not always as diplomatic as Ambassador Keller might have liked or would have liked, but we weren't the product of -- of an entirely diplomatic system either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't think it was more or less diplomatic, according to what he says here. He said: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... deliberately sacrificed." [Interpretation] Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. We were as polite as we could be, given that we had a job to do and it was important to get the job done. And there were moments when some of the diplomatic niceties had to take second place in the urgency of the situation. We were not there to get elections done any time in the next ten years. We were there on a one-year mandate with a mission that was being built up far too slowly, where the security situation was deteriorating daily. We were under constant pressure, indeed from your officials, to -- to expand our activities more, and in doing that, we may not have been quite as diplomatic as we should have been. We were perhaps more effective than we would otherwise have been by pushing forward, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In my question, I am not identifying diplomacy with courteous behaviour, but, rather, do you assume that what should use diplomatic means to achieve calm, mutual understanding and to achieve the main goal, and that is to pave the way for a peaceful settlement? Don't you consider that to be the prime aim of diplomatic efforts?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was going on in parallel, certainly throughout November and December, when Ambassador Hill was doing everything in his power to secure a separate agreement with the Kosovo Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, would you assess further explanations of your colleague who worked with you, Ambassador Keller, who says: [In English] "In a constructive atmosphere about our real problems, such as our standards of work, the interpretation of the agreement, the figures of troops, different realities on the ground. We lost whole weeks of unproductive talks about the medical evacuation helicopter, the weapons of the bodyguard, or other secondary matters. We never tried, at the upper level of the mission, to associate the Yugoslavs to our work." [Interpretation] Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is one, one opinion. I think the -- some of these issues, while small in themselves, were seen as precedents and were seen as indications of good faith or otherwise by the authorities. And when it appeared impossible to get agreement on these small issues, I think they assumed a larger importance because of their symbolic nature. There was a feeling, well, if they won't even let us fly a medical evacuation helicopter in, how are they supposed to be cooperating with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned this medical helicopter. Accidentally [as interpreted], that question was put to me personally by Mr. Walker in its time, so my question now is: Are you aware of the fact that I immediately, on the spot, when I was asked, responded by saying that we would immediately give you our own helicopter so that you can use it for the same purposes for which you planned to use the Swiss one? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it, and that was not what we were seeking. You have to remember that the OSCE member states were extremely concerned about the safety of the men and women that they made available to this mission. One of the early things we did was an assessment of the medical facilities in Kosovo, and they gave us a lot of grounds for concern. As a result of that, we wanted a properly, fully-equipped medical helicopter with a doctor and a paramedic in it available to us, and that was agreed by the permanent council of the OSCE and it was agreed that a lot of money should be spent to hire such a facility. That helicopter came as far as Skopje, having been hired, and sat on the ground in Skopje. The offer, as I understood it, was one of your helicopters which would have your insignia on it and which, in our view, would therefore be vulnerable if it was flying in areas where the Kosovo Liberation Army were. There were certainly instances of your helicopters being hit by small-arms fire, and so we did not want to end up with someone who started off being wounded, being evacuated in one of your helicopters that was subsequently shot down and a wounded man became a dead man because he happened to be in -- flying in one of your helicopters. We also had doubts as to the technical excellence of your medical evacuation helicopters. They looked rather more like helicopters with a stretcher in them rather than what we had, which was a helicopter with a fully-equipped life support system, a doctor and a paramedic. So we didn't think that like was being compared with like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a convenient moment. We will adjourn now for quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll sit now for another hour, until ten past one. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you have explained all these things about needing life support systems, paramedics, the full medical team and all the other things that attended your needs, and all these things were offered by our side without any reduction, can you answer this question: Was this helicopter supposed to be used for other purposes, other than medical, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopter had room for the doctor, the paramedic, the pilot, and the casualty. So the idea of using it for aerial reconnaissance or observation was simply out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for instance, about the statement of one of your verifiers, a Swiss national, Pascal Neuver [phoen], who said, "We understood from the beginning that the information gathered by the KVM are used for completing the information gathered by NATO via satellites. We had the impression that we were gathering intelligence for NATO." And before you answer this question, I have another related question, to save time. Are you also aware that, after this statement, this man was warned by the Swiss ministry not to speak about this again, and he said that he had received threats?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two Kosovo Verification Missions. There was a ground Kosovo Verification Mission, which was the responsibility of the OSCE, and there was an air Kosovo Verification Mission, which was the responsibility of NATO. It was, therefore, important and part of our task to talk to NATO and to exchange information. One of the things we were able to do was to ask for aerial photos of villages which -- where there had been fighting and houses had been burnt, so that we could ascertain which were the villages which were in most need of help in terms of reconstruction. Because if you drove past a village, you often saw a lot of damage on the edge of the village, but if you actually saw the air photo of it, you could see that it was confined to a narrow strip at the edge of the village. The best way of finding this sort of information out quickly on a grand scale was to do it from air photos, and that was what we would ask NATO to do on our behalf. That was entirely consistent with both our mission and NATO's mission, and we certainly were not responding to requests from NATO for information for intelligence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, really. You did or you didn't?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not respond to NATO when they requested us to get mission -- to get information specifically for intelligence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you are a NATO general, aren't you, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a general from a country that is a member of NATO, or I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. until I retired. At the time, I was assigned to the Kosovo Verification Mission I was detached from the Ministry of Defence to the British Foreign and Commonwealth office, and from there, to the OSCE, so I was not in the job as a NATO general any more than Ambassador Keller was there as a NATO diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered my previous question. Maybe it was my mistake because it was a long one. I mean the question before the helicopter, and it regarded the statement of Keller's. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... associate the Yugoslavs to our work."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that statement that you never tried to associate the Yugoslav side in your work at the upper levels?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's entirely untrue. I think we expended an enormous amount of energy attempting to gain more cooperation from the Yugoslav authorities that we dealt with. The specific example was the series of requests that were being put to the authorities in late November and early December when we were told categorically that all of this would be dealt with by Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic, in which -- which led to the meeting with -- between Sainovic and Walker at which Sainovic flatly refused all of the requests for assistance. That rather put the level of cooperation as low on the Yugoslav side rather than on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand this interpretation on your part, but this statement of Mr. Keller's with which you absolutely disagree, as you say, and you say it's completely untruthful, the statement referred to the upper levels of the mission. And he also says, [In English] "Such a work was done, sometimes very successfully, which proves that it was not an impossible challenge." That means -- I'm interested in your assessment of this cooperation at the level of Regional Centres and the efforts invested there as well as the relationships with local authorities.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that at the Regional Centres, certainly at the start, the main relationships were with the -- the local military commander and the local police commander. The relationship with the civilian authorities was slower to evolve, not least because that was something that was going to need to be developed as we got involved in the process of electoral registration, which was not starting during the winter because we didn't have the specialists available at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the accused asks his next question, where he's cross-examining on the basis of statements, it would always be helpful if we could know what the statement is, because somebody like Ambassador Keller will have probably made many statements. Alternatively, if he's going to cross-examine extensively on a particular witness statement, if he could make it available to the Chamber, to us, and particularly to the witness to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you quoting from Ambassador Keller?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gabrielle Keller -- [In English] "Gabrielle Keller, Principal Deputy Head of Mission to the Watch Group on May 25, 1999." [Interpretation] And the title is: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... mission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this annexure that you provided containing the agreement between -- this is number 2 in your table, annex under number 2, [In English] "General responsibilities, roles and missions. These reports will also be provided to authorities of the FRY." [Interpretation] And in point 3, under ii, Roman ii: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... FRY, Serbian and, as appropriate, other Kosovo authorities, political parties and other organisations in Kosovo, and accredited international and NGOs to assist in fulfilling its responsibilities." [Interpretation] And then towards the end, on the last page, it says: [In English] "Each coordination centre will maintain a liaison relationship with the opstina authorities and the local leadership." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Thus, according to the rules of the mission, you were responsible for close cooperation from the top to the bottom, from the Federal Government and the Government of Serbia, the provisional government of Kosovo, to municipal authorities. Do you believe that, on your part, you did all you could to establish that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain -- how do you understand this explanation from this official statement of Mr. Keller given to the Watch Group? [In English] "Nationals of OSCE countries not belonging to NATO who did not approve this behaviour felt more and more uncomfortable in a mission which did not reflect the sensitivity of their countries."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first thing I would say is that Mr. Keller's evidence to the Watch Group was not given under oath, and it was his opinion at the time, which was May 1999, and we all had different emotions at that stage. Having said that, the OSCE is a consensual organisation. In order to get a decision in Vienna, all the nations have to agree with it, and therefore, if any of the people in the mission felt that something was being done which trampled on their sensitivities, they had the ability to speak to their permanent delegation in Vienna and many of them did very often. Indeed, telephone lines tended to be swamped with phone calls to Vienna not coming through the secretariat but going down national lines, and quite a lot of our work was devoted to dealing with questions from individual delegations. And so there was a mechanism for any concerns to be dealt with, and that was quite regularly done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But we've just commented a moment ago on the reasons why the Italian judge, who was supposed to deal with police affairs and who considered that one needed to be easygoing and moderate in relations with the Serb police, was found to be unfit for the job.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was the task of the Kosovo Verification Mission to be easygoing on anybody. It was our job to report what we saw and to deal dispassionately with the conditions that we found, and that was what we did. I think there is a difference between going down determined to make the mission work, and go down there determined to be easygoing on any party to the dispute. We weren't there to be easygoing; we were there to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that this assertion is correct or not? Keller says: [In English] "Communication was insufficient internally and externally. Internally, very few meetings were organised for all mission members to discuss and explain the goals and means of our mission. Externally, it was still worse. The even-handedness of the mission was questioned from the very beginning. We never managed to clear this impression. By the way, did we really try?" [Interpretation] And I'm asking you the same thing. Did you really try to be unbiased?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the quick answer is yes, we thought we bent over backwards. And I think I have produced documents which show that, as late as March 1999, we were attempting still to give unbiased views of the action of the different parties involved in the conflict. Certainly in the early days, there were briefings as members came into the mission and went through the induction centre for two days. They were briefed on the mission. I personally attended all but one of induction courses at which we explained what the mission was, what its mandate was, what it was trying to do, how it should act. Various of the heads -- the Head of Mission and the Deputy Head of Mission also came down, on occasion, to the induction course and spoke to everyone there. Once people were spread out throughout the Regional Centres, obviously we couldn't bring everybody together to brief them. We certainly got everyone in Pristina together from time to time to brief them, and it was the responsibility of the Regional Centre heads to do the same for their people, and I know they worked hard at that. In terms of information going upwards, there was a constant evolution about the form of the report that was wanted in Vienna, and we did what Vienna wanted in that respect. In terms of making the report available to other organisations, that was also done, and we welcomed other non-governmental organisations at our morning briefing at 9.00 and provided them with a copy of our -- of our morning update. So I think we did do a lot to disseminate information from the start and as much as we were able to do, certainly until the last days when things got very fast-paced, and it was perhaps not possible to do that in the last days. Once we were down in Macedonia, I again went round all of the locations where the verifiers were and spoke to groups of them so that we spoke to everybody about where we thought the mission was, what the situation was, what would happen next. We put a lot of effort into briefing people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you invested efforts. Investing efforts and achieving a result are not one and the same thing. I hope you agree. Is this correct: [In English] "After some weeks of our presence, the global image of OSCE/KVM was to be anti-Serb, pro-Albanian and pro-NATO." [Interpretation] Is this claim accurate as far as your image is concerned?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was. We went out of our way to report events as they occurred as dispassionately as possible. There was certainly debate within the mission about how to describe the actions of the Kosovo Liberation Army, and it was certainly a topic that was discussed a lot, whether they should be called "terrorists" or "insurgents" or what. That was an active debate and went on for some time. You will recall that, in the press statement in the wake of the killing of the three MUP in early January, that action was firmly described as terrorist, and the discussion that went through -- went with that was -- was considerable, but that was the decision that was made, that it should be so labelled. And so I do not think that we were anti-Serb. I think we went out of our way to attempt to understand the sensitivities of the Serb population despite what we saw on the ground in terms of some difficulties in the way that particularly policemen treated Albanian civilians. We were verifying a similar agreement to NATO, and therefore we had to meet NATO and cooperate with them and they with us. We were certainly not anti-NATO. It is not the position of the OSCE to be anti-NATO. They were a partner in the -- in the process with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were leaving Kosovo, there is an impression among a certain number of mission members that Keller refers to, and he says very clearly: [In English] "I was particularly impressed by the many verifiers who showed their sadness to leave a work in which they had been totally committed during four months. They felt something more should have been done to improve the situation. They gave examples of the small success stories, especially in Regional Centres. I will mention specifically the case of Malisevo, where long talks between mission members, VJ, and MUP, as well as UCK ended successfully with the return of an important part of the population back into the town. Other long and difficult talks about the time and frequency of security patrols around the town improved the safety of the surroundings. In other places, patient efforts by highly dedicated verifiers made contacts possible again between representatives of Serbian and Albanian communities. This was needlework rather than spectacular diplomacy or verification. Many more months would have been necessary to transform those little changes into global result and to create the necessary conditions for success of these talks." [Interpretation] Do you agree with these impressions of these verifiers that your colleague is referring to?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I would associate myself with all of that statement. We had not spared ourselves in those -- those months, nearly six months in some cases, and a lot of things were done at low level which did enable things to happen, like Malisevo to have its inhabitants return to it, and we were all part of that, yes. However, at the top level, we kept encountering resistance with the officials, and they did not make our life easier. They did not work every hour that was sent to make things better, to make the job of the verifiers easier. Rather, we found that it was frustrated by the officials and our life was made more difficult. So the things that were achieved were in some cases achieved despite the recalcitrance of the officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I know full well that the government had no intention of thwarting your efforts, my question is: Which requests, apart from this one for a helicopter that you mentioned and for weapons, there was another one for weapons, can you gave us the cases when your requests were not met?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly add to those two the issue of visas, where we asked that we be given visas that were not single entry. And I recall that when my -- when my verifiers were wounded and the wounded man was transported to the border with Macedonia in one of our ambulances, and it was the intention to hand him over to a NATO ambulance that was waiting on the other side of the border, and the paramedics put him onto a stretcher and he was going to be carried on the stretcher over the border. At this point, your officials, your border officials, said, "Let me see the passport of all of the stretcher bearers." They had single-entry visas. They said, "Right. If you guys go over the line, you will not be allowed back. You will have to stay in Skopje and wait while you apply for another visa." So the wounded man had to be helped to his feet off the stretcher and stagger across the line to where he could be taken care of by the waiting medics to take him to the fully-equipped hospital. That was not cooperation on the ground. That was disgraceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not have the impression that these were substantial problems. Things of that kind happen. Visas were given, as you know, a helicopter was offered, and as far as weapons are concerned, do you know that it says in this agreement specifically, explicitly, the one I quoted a moment ago and which you have provided in annex 2, that the mission is unarmed and that is why that request was rejected, that no one should be armed. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, and the issue of sidearms for diplomatic protection people to look after Walker was the issue that became the live issue. This was particularly -- came to the fore when Walker was accosted in the street by a drunken Serb with a hand grenade in his hand in broad daylight, about 50 metres from the police station, and the police who were supposed to be policing seemed unable to deal with this situation and prevent it from happening. It was that sort of event that made Walker fear for his safety and to request that -- or to continue to request that his personal security detail be allowed sidearms. In the circumstances, I think that was reasonable, given the failure of the police on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We obviously have different opinions, but I think a fact that cannot be denied - and that brings me to my question - is whether any one of the mission members was hurt by the Serbian side during the duration of the mission, and were you well-protected by the appropriate forces of the Ministry of the Interior, including the period of your evacuation and all the other obligations that we assumed towards you as a state?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw your attention specifically to the moment when two of my verifiers were pulled out of their vehicle and were assaulted by two of your policemen. That certainly was not appropriate behaviour by those policemen. That aside, that is an isolated example, but it certainly took place, and I'm not aware of any disciplinary action or investigation taking place to do anything about it. So towards the end of the mission, there was not a feeling that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were being protected by the appropriate forces. We got the feeling that we were being denied access by the appropriate forces of the Ministry of the Interior and of the army. During the evacuation, I would specifically say that that was correctly carried out, and we were afforded every facility as we evacuated, including the provision of liaison people with communications from the Ministry of the Interior. So they get a tick for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope for other things too, because you haven't mentioned any other example except for this rough treatment by an individual policeman of whom you do not know whether he was subject to any disciplinary action or not. So in spite of everything, let us go back to the issue. Keller says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... UCK remained high." [Interpretation] Then he goes on, towards the end -- no, no, at the beginning. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... as a call to participate in the improvement of the situation on the ground. Every pullback by the Yugoslav army or the Serbian police was followed by a movement forward by its forces, which the other side, of course, considered as a violation of the ceasefire. OSCE's presence compelled the state forces to certain restraint, at least in the beginning of the mission, and UCK took advantage of this to consolidate its position." [Interpretation] Is that true? Do you agree, at least in that respect, with the author?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case in November and December, certainly in the area of Podujevo when we were building up the mission, and it was very difficult to cover everywhere at once. We also took quite a long time to establish good working communications with the UCK, because it is quite difficult to establish working communications with an insurgent underground movement. They don't have offices in the middle of the town, and they don't appear in the telephone directory. You have to go and find them. You have to make your way past wild-looking young men with their fingers on triggers, and you have to talk your way into the presence of their leaders, and that takes a lot of time and effort. It's much more difficult than simply dealing with the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is my impression correct if I say that you endeavoured mostly to establish that the Yugoslav forces were breaching the agreement and that the Albanian terrorists were doing so to a much lesser degree?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that wherever we were able to fully see a situation such as in the ambush on the border in early December, where the facts were fairly clear, then we stated what those facts were. In that case, we stated that we felt that this was a legitimate ambush by a state's armed forces and that it was a serious violation of the ceasefire by the KLA, by the UCK. In terms of the KLA coming forward into positions that had been vacated by the Yugoslav army, that certainly took -- took -- took place, and we protested it with the KLA, but at the time, we did not have very effective liaison and they choose to ignore it. Because the other thing that is difficult is that they don't have a -- quite such a good code of conduct and discipline and chain of command in an insurgent organisation as a regular army, and so you cannot expect a regular -- an irregular force to do precisely what it's told all the time, quickly, in the way that regular forces can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, your government in London had the accurate data. I assume they could only have obtained them from you. Do you know, for instance, on the 18th of January, 1999, your Minister or, rather, Secretary for Foreign Affairs in the Commonwealth, Mr. Robin Cook, at an official meeting - and I have a note on that meeting - said: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... has committed more breaches of ceasefire and until this weekend was responsible for more deaths. The Kosovo Liberation Army cannot defeat the Yugoslav army and instead of liberating the people of Kosovo, can only prolong their suffering. Neighbouring countries, in particular Albania, must be more resolute in halting the flow of weapons which fuels the conflict. The Kosovo Liberation Army has repeatedly broken the ceasefire and last month seized a number of Serb hostages." [Interpretation] So what Cook is saying, I assume, is coming, among others, from information that you provided, as you yourself said, as an officer of the Foreign Ministry, he receives. So I don't doubt that you truthfully informed your government. And what your Minister is saying is obviously at the expense of the terrorists, because that is the truth, and therefore, is it clear that there's a difference between what is truthful and what efforts were being made to prove on the ground to the effect that Serbs were permanently violating the agreement? Or maybe Cook was misinformed in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this statement, but I'm sure that he would have made it from the available information, which would have included the reports that went from ourselves up to Vienna and to the states that are part of the OSCE. I also from time to time did talk to the Foreign Ministry, because I was rung up and asked specific questions. Now, the issue on the ground was that a KLA breach of the ceasefire would be far more difficult to spot because it would be quite often small-arms fire. A Yugoslav breach of the ceasefire would often be much bigger in terms of the use of tank armament and artillery armament and, therefore, certainly a FRY breach would be much louder and would attract a lot more attention. Therefore, when the FRY forces responded, it was our opinion that that response should be proportionate, and it quite often wasn't and therefore we would report it as being disproportionate. And I recall producing documents which indicated that this use of the word "proportionality" was used really quite early in the mission and continued to be one of the features of the discussions I had with General Loncar at regular intervals. But it was not sufficient to justify the shelling of a village with the -- with the answer that there had been a terrorist there half an hour earlier. This sort of disproportionate action would -- would only get your forces into trouble, which it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you and the Americans - as you and the Americans were together - did you react proportionately in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a totally irrelevant point, a totally irrelevant point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you reacting proportionately in Iraq, when no one is attacking you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to this: A moment ago you said that you are not familiar with this statement. It is the 18th of January, 1999, Secretary of State for Foreign Commonwealth Affairs, Mr. Robin Cook said, but it wasn't just a statement, it was a meeting attended by others as well. For instance, Mr. John Randolf, Uxbridge - probably an MP from that area, I assume - says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... sanctions and threats used against Belgrade. What sanctions and threats could be used against the KLA?" [Interpretation] And then he's given the answer that you most emphatically condemned, that all international furor, and so on and so forth, but as you know, this was not productive. And therefore, London was fully aware of the situation regarding consequences and background. Are you aware of what Mr. Cook says now: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... in all its different manifestations, including the European Union, the Contact Group and the Security Council, is that we do not support independence for Kosovo. That is partly because the countries in the neighbourhood would strongly resent and resist any attempt to establish an independent Kosovo because --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker be asked to read more slowly please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to read the English more slowly, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll keep track of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Always remember that the agenda of the KLA is not independence for Kosovo but a Greater Albania. It would also have an effect in Bosnia about which all honourable members should be concerned. It would be very difficult to resist the demand of Republika Srpska for independence if Kosovo were to secede --" not to secede -- "if Kosovo were to succeed in achieving it." [Interpretation] And now we come to a very important statement which I would like to ask you about. In response to Mr. Cook said, Mr. Dave Campbell Davis [phoen], from Washington, says: [In English] "Is not the bottom line the fact that the KLA, in pursuing its objective of Greater Albania is making decision taking in a NATO, taking in a NATO extremely difficult --" [Interpretation] You didn't interpret that correctly. "... taking in NATO becomes extremely difficult." [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... cannot take any military action in Kosovo..."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the point that is being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... the KLA will be solely to blame because it will have prevented such action." [Interpretation] My question is: Is this sufficient to show - because obviously the speaker is aware of the planned NATO activities - is this sufficient to show that the war against Yugoslavia had already been decided about? Because this meeting was held on the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and I was not in NATO at that stage, there was not any decision of that nature at that stage. There may well have been contingency planning, because that's what NATO does. It has contingency plans for all areas of NATO, from one end to the other. And if you're a military organisation, that's your professional job, so that you can deal with a situation as it arises, without saying, "Gosh, we've just noticed this, we haven't got a plan." That was the problem we had in Vienna in October, that we had to start to plan with the clock ticking, after the mandate had started. So whatever NATO was doing at the time in the form of planning, I believe it was normal planning that any sensible organisation does if it has the capacity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you saw here that because of the obvious breaches by the Albanians, there was a danger, as Mr. Dave Campbell Davis [phoen] says, that this could spoil or undermine the reasons for NATO going in, for NATO carrying out its plan. He says very well here: [In English] "NATO cannot take any military actions then in Kosovo." [Interpretation] If they behave in this way and that they would be to blame for preventing NATO from taking military action by their behaviour. That is why I'm asking you: Is this not sufficient proof that the intention to go to war already existed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that as best he can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Cook responded: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... on more than one occasion this afternoon there is fault on both sides and the KLA must accept its responsibility for the present situation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's too fast, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Too fast. Can you read it again so that they can get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "As I have said on more than one occasion this afternoon, there is fault on both sides, and the KLA must accept its responsibility for the present situation because of its repeated breaches of the ceasefire." [Interpretation] And then -- so this was on the 18th of January. That means after all these dramatic events that you have described, and he says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Kosovo Verification Mission for securing the release today of eight members of the Yugoslav army taken prisoners taken by Kosovo -- taken prisoner by Kosovo Liberation Army on 8th of January." [Interpretation] And then he adds: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... the UCK not to repeat this irresponsible action. We welcome the restraint demonstrated on this occasion by the FRY Serb security forces which allowed the KVM successfully to negotiate the release of the abducted men. This restraint must continue throughout the whole Kosovo." [Interpretation] Does this show that, at that point in time, and we're talking about the 18th of January, even Cook was not aware of the fact that Racak would be used as the trigger for the war? What is your opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can deal with that. You must ask Mr. Cook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, yes. Briefly, please, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In talking about the restraint that had been demonstrated by the security forces when we were getting the eight soldiers off the hill, I do recall at one stage that I had to withdraw my people who were standing between the two sides because the order was being passed that an assault should go in by the security forces. And so there was restraint in that we did manage eventually to get a successful conclusion to it, but it was extremely hard. And it was made harder by the extremely awkward attitude of -- of the Serb security forces who kept us under constant pressure in this respect, not only forcing me to pull my people back on at least one occasion but also, as I think I mentioned, producing a column headed for Kosovo which looked extremely like special forces on their way. All of these things made it an extremely difficult and trying time. So I would qualify the description of the restraint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The substance of the question I put to you really relates to a decision that had already been taken to find a reason for the war. And in this connection, you said yesterday something of importance, an important testimony that fits into what your MP was saying, talking to Mr. Cook, that the KLA would prevent NATO from achieving its goal. You said that you entered Mr. Walker's office when he was calling up Mr. Holbrooke after Racak, and you quoted his words. I took note of them very carefully. "You can kiss your Nobel Peace Prize away." In other words, "We found an excuse for the war." "You can kiss your Nobel Prize goodbye. We found a reason for the war." Is it clear that Walker's task was to create conditions for the war?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, and that's not my interpretation of what I heard him say. He was extremely stressed. He was talking to someone who he clearly knew very well, and he was feeling extremely frustrated. I think you should ask him what he meant by it, but it wasn't my interpretation that this was going to be an excuse for starting a war. And anyone you asked in the Kosovo Verification Mission would -- would disagree with you on that. We were determined to continue to make this mission work for as long as humanly possible, and every one of us was personally dedicated to that, and we put ourselves into some very difficult situations in order to attempt to continue to do that right up to the moment we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was the feeling of the majority of mission members, but this was a conversation between two individuals who knew what they were talking about. Nothing would come of peace and, "We have an excuse for the war." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Does that explain another of Keller's assessments, one generally shared, that the KLA used the restraint of Yugoslavia and the Serb security forces to consolidate itself?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- the KLA did consolidate itself over that winter to a degree, and that is seen by the -- the column that was ambushed in early December, which had, as we understand it, about 140 people, each with a pack full of munitions with him. So yes, they were doing that. But that was not, in our view, a -- a cause for disproportionate response by the security forces. Two wrongs do not make a right, and what is -- what an insurgent organisation does is not an excuse for regular security forces to mimic it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will more light be cast on this fact with a quotation from an interview granted by the chief of the bandits - they call him a commander- Ramush Hajradinaj [phoen], who gave this interview in 1999 to Azari [phoen], and he says: "The agreement signed by Holbrooke has saved the KLA. The arrival of the OSCE verifiers in Kosovo has enabled the revival of the UCK. We need to bear in mind that because of the difficult situation that we were in, we wanted a breather, and in concrete terms, this agreement was salvation for the OVK, especially for the Dukagjinii area." That is how they call Metohija. "The agreement was of decisive importance, and it assisted us a great deal to revive the army." What is your impression? To what extent did you really assist them in reviving their army?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that was our view of what our job was. I certainly know, with the benefit of hindsight, that there was work done to reinforce them over this period, but the purpose of the whole mission was to buy time for a diplomatic solution, for a solution that involved an election, and that's what we thought we were there for, rather than to act as -- as any party that was in any way favouring the Kosovo Liberation Army. That was emphatically not our perception of our role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you see what he goes on to say. He mentions you. I don't mean you personally. He speaks about specific meetings with verifiers, and he says, in reference to those meetings: "We went further than discussing current topics and events. Our discussions went on to cover our ideas, the ways in which we intend to realise our goal, up to the need for cooperation of the KLA and other factors. Usually the lengthiest discussions were conducted with the military observers, especially with those from Britain, America, France, Canada, and other observers. They studied the goals, opinions, and ideas, and there were separate pre-preparations of NATO for the airstrikes that were to follow."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just put the question a moment ago, and I am just elaborating on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To what extent did the KVM assist in the strengthening or, as he put it, "It helped us to revive or resuscitate the army"? And we see the context and the purpose of it. A moment ago, your answer was that you did not act in that direction, but he is denying that with this explanation and reference to talks with observers, military observers especially, of various armies, English, American, and so on. I don't need to read that again. So was it like that or not? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the job of the officers that I -- or the people that I assigned to be liaison with the Kosovo Liberation Army, to get to know them and to assess as part of their job what the strength and the possible intentions of the Kosovo Liberation Army was. And therefore, they had to have discussions with them, yes. They had to earn the trust of the Kosovo Liberation Army in the same way that the people I put with the VJ and the MUP had to earn the trust of the VJ and the MUP. That meant, for instance, that we did not reveal the locations that they had gone to. We didn't do it with the VJ and MUP, and we didn't do it with the Kosovo Liberation Army. And so these liaison officers dealt with one set of people, and trust was built up so that a proper assessment could be made of what the likely intentions were of these people. The use that they put the period that we were there to is obviously up to them. The period we were there was also an opportunity for Yugoslavia to have put into place the conditions that they were talking about in one of the early documents about establishing a multi-ethnic police force with representation from all the ethnic groups. You could have been doing that while the KLA were doing their work and that would have probably eroded support for the KLA, but you chose not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to call it a day there. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock Monday morning. General, would you be back then, please, to continue your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The supplementary report of the last witness, Riedlmayer, 88A, is now available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could hand it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
